title: Tissue Repair, Wound Healing & Fibrosis · Board-Ready

sources.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Principles of Wound Healing

questions.question: Three days after an uncomplicated laceration repair, the wound contains neutrophils, macrophages, early granulation tissue, and proliferating fibroblasts. Which interpretation is most accurate?
choices: Healing phases overlap; inflammation is transitioning into proliferation rather than occurring as isolated blocks
The presence of macrophages proves chronic infection
Fibroblasts appear only after remodeling is complete
Granulation tissue indicates irreversible wound failure
rationales: Hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling overlap, so several cell types and processes can coexist.
Macrophages are normal participants in debris clearance and repair signaling.
Fibroblasts are central during proliferation and matrix deposition before mature remodeling.
Granulation tissue with capillaries and fibroblasts is expected in repair.
questions.explanation: Clinical wound assessment should recognize overlapping biology while looking for deviations such as spreading infection, ischemia, or dehiscence.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes has a plantar ulcer, diminished protective sensation, callus, and weak pedal pulses. Which plan best addresses major barriers to healing?
choices: Assess perfusion and infection, offload pressure, optimize metabolic factors, and arrange appropriate wound/vascular follow-up
Debride aggressively without first considering ischemia or depth
Recommend continued full weight bearing to increase local pressure
Treat only the serum glucose because neuropathy and perfusion do not affect healing
rationales: Healing depends on perfusion, pressure relief, infection control, metabolic status, and coordinated wound care.
Debridement strategy must consider perfusion, tissue viability, infection, and anatomy.
Continued pressure perpetuates injury in a neuropathic plantar ulcer.
Neuropathy, repetitive trauma, and arterial disease can be as important as glycemic status.
questions.explanation: A complex wound is rarely solved by one intervention; advanced reasoning identifies and corrects multiple barriers.

questions.question: Seven days after abdominal surgery, a patient reports a sudden pulling sensation followed by pink fluid from the incision. Which concern is most urgent?
choices: Wound dehiscence during a period of limited tensile strength
Normal remodeling with fully restored tissue strength
Keloid formation confined beyond the incision
Immediate type I hypersensitivity to collagen
rationales: Early wounds have low tensile strength; sudden serosanguineous drainage and separation symptoms raise concern for dehiscence.
Tensile strength is far from fully restored at one week.
Keloids develop over time as excessive scar tissue, not as sudden drainage.
The presentation is mechanical wound failure, not collagen allergy.
questions.explanation: Possible dehiscence requires prompt surgical assessment; if organs protrude, protect the area and activate emergency care rather than attempting reduction.

questions.question: A patient with a severely restricted diet has gingival bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhage, and poor wound strength. Which impaired repair process is most likely?
choices: Defective vitamin C–dependent collagen hydroxylation and stabilization
Excess vitamin K–dependent elastin cross-linking
Failure of C9 to form a membrane attack complex
Increased keratinocyte ATP production
rationales: Vitamin C is required for collagen proline and lysine hydroxylation; deficiency weakens connective tissue and healing.
Vitamin K supports coagulation-factor modification, not elastin cross-linking as described.
Terminal complement does not explain the connective-tissue pattern.
The problem is collagen integrity rather than excess ATP production.
questions.explanation: Nutritional deficiencies can present through the biology of repair; correcting the substrate deficit is part of treatment.

questions.question: A smoker's surgical wound is healing slowly despite no overt infection. Which mechanism most plausibly contributes?
choices: Nicotine-related vasoconstriction and carbon-monoxide–related reduction in oxygen delivery impair oxygen-dependent repair
Smoking selectively increases fibroblast proliferation and collagen strength
Tobacco exposure eliminates neutrophil proteases from the wound
Carbon monoxide increases hemoglobin oxygen release to ischemic tissue
rationales: Smoking can reduce tissue oxygenation and impair inflammatory and fibroblast function, delaying repair.
The net effect is impaired rather than enhanced matrix formation.
Smoking does not simply eliminate neutrophil proteases and can dysregulate host defense.
Carbon monoxide increases hemoglobin affinity and reduces oxygen-carrying capacity rather than improving delivery.
questions.explanation: Oxygen is needed for bacterial killing, collagen processing, and cell metabolism; smoking affects several points in this pathway.

questions.question: Months after ear piercing, a firm scar grows beyond the original wound borders and continues enlarging. Which diagnosis is most likely?
choices: Keloid caused by excessive scar deposition extending beyond the initial injury
Hypertrophic scar that by definition extends far beyond the wound
Wound dehiscence caused by insufficient collagen
Granulation tissue from normal primary intention
rationales: Keloids extend beyond the original injury and may continue growing.
Hypertrophic scars remain within the original wound boundaries and may regress.
Dehiscence is separation from inadequate strength, not an enlarging raised scar.
Granulation tissue is an earlier repair tissue and does not describe this mature overgrowth.
questions.explanation: Both keloids and hypertrophic scars involve excess matrix, but border behavior and natural history distinguish them.

questions.question: A bedbound patient develops nonblanchable sacral erythema with intact skin. What intervention most directly addresses the initiating injury?
choices: Prompt pressure redistribution and regular repositioning while assessing nutrition, moisture, and perfusion
Massage the erythematous prominence vigorously to increase friction
Continue the same position until the skin opens for accurate staging
Apply systemic antibiotics despite no evidence of infection
rationales: Relieving sustained pressure is central before deeper ischemic damage develops; other modifiable risks should also be addressed.
Vigorous massage can worsen tissue injury over a pressure point.
Waiting permits progression and is unsafe.
Antibiotics do not treat pressure injury without infection.
questions.explanation: Nonblanchable erythema is an early warning of pressure-related tissue injury and should trigger immediate prevention and support measures.

questions.question: A patient has a shallow medial-ankle ulcer, edema, varicosities, and hemosiderin staining. Pedal pulses are difficult to assess. What should occur before routine high-compression treatment?
choices: Evaluate arterial perfusion because significant arterial disease can make strong compression unsafe
Assume venous disease excludes arterial disease
Use compression only after the wound has completely epithelialized
Avoid leg elevation because it increases venous pressure
rationales: The pattern suggests venous disease, but arterial status should be assessed when uncertain because mixed disease changes compression safety.
Venous and arterial disease can coexist, especially in older adults.
Appropriate compression is often part of venous-ulcer healing rather than something reserved until closure.
Elevation generally lowers venous hydrostatic pressure when clinically appropriate.
questions.explanation: Pattern recognition suggests venous hypertension, but safe planning confirms that arterial inflow can tolerate the proposed intervention.

questions.question: A patient with chronic liver injury develops progressive architectural distortion from fibrosis. Which mediator-cell relationship is most central?
choices: Persistent TGF-β–dominant signaling activates matrix-producing cells and reduces normal matrix resolution
Histamine converts hepatocytes directly into collagen fibers
Neutrophils permanently replace hepatic stellate cells
C3b enzymatically digests all extracellular matrix
rationales: TGF-β is a major profibrotic signal that increases extracellular-matrix production and favors scar persistence.
Histamine does not convert cells into collagen fibers.
Neutrophils may participate in inflammation but do not replace the matrix-producing cell population.
Complement does not remove all matrix in this manner.
questions.explanation: Fibrosis reflects an imbalance between matrix production and degradation during persistent injury, not simply the presence of inflammation.

questions.question: Which wound is most likely to heal by secondary intention?
choices: A contaminated ulcer with tissue loss and edges that cannot be approximated
A clean surgical incision with closely apposed edges
A superficial paper cut immediately closed with adhesive
A laparoscopic port closed primarily without infection
rationales: Substantial tissue loss and nonapposed edges require granulation, contraction, and epithelialization from the wound margins.
A clean apposed incision typically heals by primary intention with less granulation and contraction.
A small approximated superficial cut behaves more like primary healing.
A primarily closed clean port does not require secondary-intention filling unless complicated.
questions.explanation: Secondary intention demands more granulation tissue and contraction and generally produces a larger scar than primary intention.
